A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, Optimal Regularization for Performative Learning. Their complete text, equations, figures, table, and appendices are readable. The original results and proofs can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original Gaussian simulations and Housing and LSAC regression experiments in Figures 1–4, with experimental details in Appendix D.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds neural-network classification results, alternative-regularizer experiments, and empirical covariance analyses.

M1.justification: The central ridge estimator and repeated risk minimization procedure remain unchanged. v2 adds empirical training variants using dropout, Lasso, and elastic net, and applies L2 regularization to a neural-network classifier. These extend the instantiated procedures without replacing the central method.

E1.justification: Gaussian simulations, Housing, and LSAC are retained. Section 6 adds GiveMeSomeCredit binary classification with strategic modification of manipulable features, substantially extending coverage beyond regression with synthetic label shifts. The sub-Gaussian extension is theoretical, not an additional empirical dataset.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates ridge regularization only. v2 Appendix A evaluates dropout, Lasso, and elastic net on the same Housing and LSAC settings and compares their behavior with ridge in Figure 4. This adds three alternative regularization families; Mofakhami et al. supplies the neural-network setup rather than a separately evaluated competing algorithm.

E3.justification: The original ridge experiments retain their splits, sample sizes, and retraining settings. The added neural-network experiment introduces convergence-based dynamics, strategic feature-copying controlled by delta, regularization sweeps, and final test accuracy. Appendix A also adds controlled replacement of the regularizer within the retained regression settings.

E4.justification: Figures 6–8 newly test whether the observed behavior depends on using ridge by substituting three other regularizers. The neural-network experiment probes applicability beyond linear regression. Appendix G adds covariance heatmaps and examines departures from the simplified covariance structure used in the theory.

E5.justification: v2 newly specifies shared randomness across delta and lambda and repeated runs for the neural-network experiment, although the count is only described as 'several times'. Existing trial counts and one-standard-deviation reporting are retained. There is no documented increase in runs for the original experiments or new significance-testing procedure.

E6.justification: Figures 1–4 retain their original results. v2 adds neural-network accuracy curves showing mitigation through L2 regularization, nine regression panels for alternative regularizers, and empirical covariance estimates. These are substantial new results under added methods and settings, not improved ridge scores under the original conditions. Figure 6(c)'s caption incorrectly says the optimal dropout rate increases, while the plotted optima move downward.

T1.justification: The original principal results remain as Theorem 4.1, Corollary 4.2, and Theorems 5.1–5.2. New Appendix D provides a sub-Gaussian extension with additional coefficient and initialization assumptions and a weaker probability guarantee. New Appendix F defines risk against the shifted training distribution and derives its deterministic equivalent, optimal regularization, and risk-sign results. v2 also explicitly discusses applicability to non-diagonal performative matrices.

C1.justification: The central claims about population versus proportional regimes and regularization scaling are retained. The introduction's third contribution now explicitly claims empirical applicability beyond the theoretical assumptions and to other regularizers. The abstract additionally attributes the over-parameterized benefit to reduced parameter-estimation variance.

C2.justification: v2 explains how conclusions depend on evaluating the untouched or shifted distribution and adds societal tradeoffs for both choices in the Impact Statement. It also adds feature-shift limitations, an informal Bayesian explanation, and interpretations of alternative-regularizer behavior. The shifted-risk summary in Section 5 omits the kappa >= 2 restrictions attached to some appendix sign results.

D1.justification: v2 documents use of whynot and Mofakhami et al.'s code and largest network, and specifies equal L1/L2 weighting for elastic net. The original preprocessing, feature table, and repository address remain. The single-laptop hardware disclosure is removed. Exact neural-network architecture and hyperparameter values are largely delegated to the cited setup rather than supplied locally.

R1.justification: Related work expands to initial-distribution evaluation, label shifts, and difficulties learning performative effects in high dimensions. The novelty statement changes from model choice being unstudied to a claimed first use of high-dimensional statistical tools. New citations include Mofakhami, Clara, Demirel, Tsoy, and Bracale; Cheng and Montanari is removed. The main intellectual foundation remains intact.

P1.justification: The seven-section main narrative and much of its wording are retained. v2 makes targeted explanatory rewrites, removes the main-text proof sketch while retaining the full proof, reorganizes the appendices, and adds Impact and Conflict of Interest statements. Affiliations and publication headers change, and an unresolved '(??)' reference appears in Appendix E.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the single-column main text with a two-column conference layout and substantially rearranges figure placement. It retains Figures 1–4 and Table 1 while adding the neural-network plot, three multi-panel regularizer figures, and two covariance heatmaps. These constitute substantial visual and layout changes.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the paper by extending its Gaussian theory, analyzing an alternative evaluation distribution, and testing applicability beyond linear ridge regression. Appendix F makes the dependence of conclusions on the risk criterion explicit, while Figures 5–8 provide broader empirical support. These gains outweigh localized weaknesses: incomplete neural-network reproduction details, omitted conditions in the shifted-risk summary, and the incorrect dropout-direction caption in Figure 6(c).
